name: No-Bake Maple Oat Energy Balls
description: Soft, poppable oat, nut butter and maple balls with mini chocolate chips. They travel well in a vest pocket.
ingredients: 90 g smooth peanut or almond butter
40 g mini dark chocolate chips (or raisins in hot weather)
steps: Warm the nut butter and maple syrup in the microwave for 20 seconds so they blend easily.
Stir in the oats and salt until you have a sticky dough. Add a spoonful of oats if it's too wet, or a splash of water if it's too dry.
Once the dough is cool, fold in the chocolate chips so they don't melt.
Chill for 15 minutes, then roll into 12 balls of about 30 g each with damp hands.
Wrap them in pairs in foil or baking paper for the trail.
tip: Eat one every 20-30 minutes with water. Two or three an hour covers part of a 30-60 g/hour carb target; add drink carbs on top.
storage: Keeps for 1 week in the fridge, and 1-2 days in a vest in cool weather.

name: Date and Almond Energy Bars
description: A homemade take on shop-bought fruit-and-nut bars: dense, chewy, naturally sweet, made from real food, and gluten-free.
steps: If the dates are firm, soak them in hot water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat them dry.
Pulse the almonds in a food processor to coarse crumbs and tip them out. This keeps some texture in the bars.
Blitz the dates for 1-2 minutes to a sticky paste.
Add the almonds, oats, cocoa and salt and pulse until the mixture clumps together.
Press it very firmly into a 450 g (1 lb) loaf tin lined with baking paper and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Cut into 10 bars and wrap each one in foil or baking paper.
tip: The almonds add fat and fibre, so these suit long, steady efforts and the first half of an ultra better than hard racing.
storage: Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

name: Nut Butter Rice Cakes
description: Sticky rice pressed with nut butter, honey and salt, in the style long popular in pro cycling. Soft and easy on the stomach.
steps: Rinse the rice, then bring it to the boil with the water. Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest it off the heat, lid on, for 10 minutes.
While it's still hot, stir through the nut butter, honey and salt until evenly coated.
Press it firmly into a 20 cm tin lined with baking paper, about 2 cm thick, using a damp spatula.
Cool, then chill for 1 hour.
Cut into 8 squares and wrap each one in foil, twisting the ends so it's easy to open mid-run.
tip: Rice is low in fibre and gentle on the gut, which makes it a good first solid food in a long race.
storage: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge.

name: Salted Sweet Potato Bites
description: Soft roasted sweet potato cubes, salted generously. Whole-food carbs that sit gently when sweet gels stop working.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C fan (220°C / 425°F).
Peel the sweet potatoes and cut them into 2 cm cubes.
Toss with the oil and a generous pinch of salt and spread them in a single layer on a lined tray.
Roast for 25-30 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and caramelised at the edges.
Cool completely before bagging them; packed warm, they steam and go mushy.
tip: Savoury-sweet real food for the stage when gels stop going down. Eat a few cubes every 20-30 minutes.
storage: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge.

name: Honey Nut Butter Tortilla Roll
description: A soft tortilla spread with nut butter, honey and salt, rolled tight and sliced into pinwheels for the trail.
steps: Lay the tortilla flat and spread the nut butter thinly right to the edges.
Drizzle over the honey and sprinkle with the salt.
Roll it up tightly.
Either wrap the whole roll in foil and twist the ends, or cut it into 4 pinwheels and pack them in a small box.
tip: Pinwheels let you eat a quarter at a time. The fat and protein make it slower-burning, better for long, easy miles than hard racing.

name: Peanut Butter Banana Sushi
description: A banana coated in peanut butter, rolled in oats and sliced into bite-size rounds. Pre-run, mid-hike or post-run.
ingredients: 15 g rolled oats or puffed rice
steps: Peel the banana and coat it all over in a thin layer of peanut butter.
Roll it in the oats until covered.
Slice it into 2 cm rounds.
Pack them flat in a small container so they don't squash.
tip: Best eaten within a few hours. It's ideal for hikes and long, easy runs rather than racing.

name: DIY Trail Mix
description: The salty-sweet classic: raisins, salted peanuts, mini pretzels and dark chocolate, portioned into small bags.
steps: Combine everything in a large bowl. If your peanuts are unsalted, add a small pinch of salt.
Toss well so the salt and chocolate are evenly spread.
Divide into 8 small zip bags of about 55 g each.
tip: The salted peanuts and pretzels bring sodium, and the raisins bring quick carbs. The fat means it's better on long, slow days than in a fast race.
storage: Keeps for 1 month in a cool, dry place.

name: Salted Boiled Potatoes
description: Baby potatoes boiled until tender and rolled in flaky salt. The classic ultra aid-station food.
steps: Scrub the potatoes and boil them in well-salted water for 12-15 minutes until just tender.
Drain and let them steam-dry for 5 minutes.
While they're still warm, toss them with the oil and roll them in the flaky salt.
Cool, then pack them into a container or bags.
tip: About 20 g of carbs and a good dose of sodium per bag. Rotate them with sweet foods to beat flavour fatigue.
storage: Keeps for 1 day at room temperature or 3 days in the fridge.

name: Homemade Electrolyte Drink
description: A simple homemade sports drink with fruit juice, sugar and salt. About 40 g carbs and 575 mg sodium per 750 ml bottle.
ingredients: 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar or maple syrup
Squeeze of fresh lemon or lime
steps: Dissolve the sugar and salt in the warm water first, so there's no grit.
Pour it into a 750 ml bottle with the juice and cold water.
Add a squeeze of citrus, seal and shake well.
Chill it before you head out.
tip: A solid starting point for hot or long efforts. A trained gut can handle a stronger mix (up to about 60 g carbs per bottle), but test it in training first.

name: Pumpkin Seed Cranberry Oat Bars
description: Chewy baked oat bars with pumpkin seeds and cranberries, bound with honey and butter.
steps: Heat the oven to 170°C fan (190°C / 375°F) and line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper.
Gently melt the butter, honey and salt together without letting it boil.
Stir in the oats, pumpkin seeds and cranberries until every oat is coated.
Press the mixture very firmly into the tin; loosely packed flapjack crumbles.
Bake for 20-22 minutes, until golden at the edges.
Score into 9 while warm, then let it cool completely in the tin before cutting through.
tip: Sturdy enough for a vest pocket. Eat half a bar every 30 minutes on long, steady runs.
storage: Keeps for 1 week in an airtight tin.

name: Peanut-Stuffed Dates
description: Soft Medjool dates filled with peanut butter and topped with flaky salt. Two ingredients, three minutes.
steps: Slice each date lengthways and pull out the stone.
Spoon a little peanut butter into each opening.
Pinch it closed and press a few flakes of salt on top.
Pack them snugly in a small tub, or wrap them in pairs, so the filling stays put.
tip: Each date is about 18 g of carbs. They're easy to chew and swallow on the move, and the salt and peanut butter stop them tasting sickly.

name: Banana and Oat Trail Cookies
description: Three-ingredient soft cookies of banana, oats and raisins with cinnamon. No added sugar, and they don't crumble.
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C fan (200°C / 400°F) and line a tray.
Mash the bananas thoroughly, then stir in the oats, raisins, cinnamon and salt until thick and evenly combined.
Spoon 10 mounds onto the tray and flatten them slightly with the back of a spoon.
Bake for 15 minutes, until set and lightly golden.
Cool completely before stacking them.
tip: Low-fat, gentle carbs. Two cookies make roughly one gel's worth of carbohydrate.
storage: Keeps for 3 days in a tin or 1 month in the freezer.

name: Puffed Rice and Honey Bars
description: Light, crisp bars of puffed rice bound with honey and peanut butter. Like a grown-up crispy cake.
steps: Warm the honey and peanut butter in a pan over a low heat for 1-2 minutes, until runny and just bubbling at the edges. The brief simmer helps the bars set firm.
Take it off the heat and stir in the salt.
Fold in the puffed rice until every grain is coated.
Press it firmly into a lined loaf tin and chill for 1 hour.
Cut into 8 bars and wrap them individually.
tip: Low in fibre and quick to digest: a good mid-race bar. Keep them cool and they won't fall apart in a pocket.
storage: Keeps for 1 week in the fridge.

name: Coconut Sticky Rice Bites
description: Chewy glutinous rice balls soaked in sweet, salty coconut milk and rolled in toasted coconut. A welcome change from gels.
steps: Soak the rice in cold water for at least 1 hour, or overnight, then drain.
Steam it in a steamer or sieve lined with muslin over simmering water for 20-25 minutes, until translucent and chewy. Or simmer it as the packet says.
Warm the coconut milk with the maple syrup and salt and stir it into the hot rice. Cover and leave for 10 minutes to absorb.
With damp hands, shape the rice into 8 balls and roll them in the toasted coconut.
Wrap each ball in cling film so it stays moist in your vest.
tip: A flavour change for hour three onwards, when everything sweet starts to taste the same.
storage: Best eaten within 24 hours. Keep them cool.

name: Rice Pudding Pouch
description: Smooth, cinnamon-scented rice pudding spooned into reusable pouches. Carbs you can squeeze when chewing feels like work.
steps: Simmer the rice with the milk, honey, cinnamon and salt for 8-10 minutes, stirring, until thick and creamy.
Blend it briefly until smooth so it squeezes easily.
Cool it completely.
Spoon it into reusable pouches or a soft flask (a funnel or piping bag helps) and chill until needed.
tip: Keep it in a cool pocket and eat it within about 4 hours of leaving the fridge; it's dairy.

name: Miso Rice Balls
description: Onigiri-style rice balls seasoned with miso and salt. A savoury, easy-to-swallow fuel for when you can't face another sweet bite.
ingredients: 370 g warm cooked sushi rice (from 150 g uncooked)
steps: Dissolve the miso in the hot water and stir it through the warm rice.
Wet your hands and rub a little salt over your palms.
Take about 60 g of rice, tuck a few sesame seeds into the middle, and press it firmly into a compact triangle or ball.
Wrap a nori strip around it if you like (it softens over time), then wrap each ball tightly in cling film.
Keep them cool and eat them the same day.
tip: Salty, savoury carbs that go down easily late in a race. Make them the night before.

name: Mashed Potato Salt Flask
description: Silky salted mashed potato in a squeezable pouch. Real-food carbs and sodium without any chewing.
ingredients: 3 medium potatoes (about 450 g), peeled and chunked
steps: Boil the potatoes for 15-20 minutes until completely soft, then drain.
Mash them with the oil, salt and enough warm water to make a smooth, spoonable paste.
Push it through a sieve for a truly lump-free texture; lumps block pouch spouts.
While it's still warm, spoon it into reusable pouches or soft flasks. Sip it slowly rather than taking big mouthfuls.
tip: One of the best late-race foods when your stomach is rebelling. It's savoury and salty and needs no chewing.
storage: Keeps for 1 day in the fridge.

name: Maple Lemon Carb Drink
description: A simple maple syrup, lemon and salt drink with about 60 g of carbohydrate per 500 ml bottle.
steps: Dissolve the maple syrup and salt in a little warm water in a 500 ml bottle.
Top it up with cold water and add the lemon juice.
Shake well before each sip, because the syrup settles.
tip: Sip it steadily through an hour alongside solid food. At this strength, rehearse it in training before race day.

name: Carb-Load Tomato Rice
description: A slightly soupy, mild tomato rice for the night before a long race. Lots of carbs, very little fibre or spice.
steps: Soften the onion in the oil for 5 minutes without letting it brown.
Add the garlic and paprika for 30 seconds.
Stir in the rice for 1 minute.

Add the passata, stock, sugar and salt. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on a low heat for 15-18 minutes, stirring once or twice and adding a splash of water if it dries out. You want it slightly soupy.
Stir in the Parmesan and basil.
tip: Eat it early enough to digest; finish at least 12 hours before the start. Rehearse it before a long training run.

name: Beetroot and Feta Pre-Race Rice
description: Basmati rice turned pink with balsamic-warmed beetroot, finished with feta, dill and lemon.
ingredients: 250 g cooked beetroot (vacuum-packed, not in vinegar), diced
Small handful of dill or mint
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it with 270 ml water and a pinch of salt: bring it to the boil, cover, cook on a low heat for 10 minutes, then rest it for 5.
Meanwhile, warm the beetroot with the oil and balsamic in a pan for 3 minutes.
Stir the beetroot through the rice until it turns pink.
Crumble over the feta, scatter with herbs and squeeze over the lemon.
tip: Beetroot is rich in dietary nitrate, which has modest evidence for improving endurance efficiency. Many runners eat it daily for several days before a race. Harmless side effect: pink urine.

name: Race-Morning Overnight Oats
description: Low-fibre, low-fat overnight oats with banana, honey and raisins, made the night before so there's nothing to cook at 4 a.m.
steps: Mash the banana in a jar.
Stir in the oats, milk, honey, raisins, salt and cinnamon.
Put the lid on and refrigerate overnight.
Eat it cold, straight from the jar, 2.5-3 hours before the start.
tip: No chia, nuts or protein powder, on purpose: keep race-morning fibre and fat low. It has about 70 g of carbs; for bigger runners or longer races, add a slice of toast with honey.

name: Date and Cocoa Trail Balls
description: Nut-free, almost fat-free balls of dates, oats and cocoa. Soft to chew and quick to digest on the move.
steps: If the dates are firm, soak them in hot water for 10 minutes and drain them well.
Blitz the oats in a food processor to a coarse flour.
Add the dates, cocoa, salt and orange juice and process until the mixture forms a ball.
Roll it into 12 balls with damp hands, and dust them in extra cocoa if you like.
Chill for 20 minutes, then wrap them in pairs.
tip: Being nut-free and very low in fat, they digest faster than most bars. One every 20-30 minutes is a good rhythm.
storage: Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

name: Salted Maple Rice Cakes
description: Sticky rice pressed with maple syrup, lemon zest and flaky salt. Nut-free, fat-free and very gentle on the gut.
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it with the water: bring it to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest it for 10.
While it's hot, stir through the maple syrup, lemon zest and half the salt.
Press it firmly into a lined 20 cm tin, about 2 cm thick, and sprinkle over the remaining salt.
Chill for 1 hour, cut into 8 squares, and wrap each one in foil or rice paper.
tip: A great first solid food of a race when your stomach is unsettled.
storage: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge.

name: Salted Banana Bread Bites
description: Dense banana bread with extra salt baked in, cut into cubes. Real food that still feels like a treat deep into a long run.
steps: Heat the oven to 160°C fan (180°C / 350°F) and line a 900 g (2 lb) loaf tin.
Mash the bananas well, then whisk in the melted butter, sugar and eggs.
Fold in the flour, bicarbonate of soda, salt and cinnamon until no streaks of flour remain.
Pour it into the tin and bake for 50-60 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean. Cover it loosely with foil after 35 minutes if it's browning fast.
Cool completely, then cut into 16 cubes, press a few salt flakes onto each, and wrap them in pairs.
tip: The extra salt is intentional: about 150 mg of sodium per bite on top of about 20 g of carbs.
storage: Keeps for 3 days wrapped, or 1 month in the freezer. Take them straight from the freezer for a morning long run.

name: Apricot and Almond Energy Bars
description: No-bake bars of dried apricot, almonds, oats, honey and orange zest. They hold their shape in a hot vest pocket.
steps: Pulse the almonds to coarse crumbs and tip them out.
Process the apricots, honey and orange zest to a sticky paste.
Add the almonds, oats and salt and pulse until combined.
Press the mixture firmly into a lined loaf tin and chill for 1 hour.
Cut into 10 bars and wrap them individually.
tip: Apricots are one of the best dried fruits for potassium. These pack a lot of carbs per gram.
storage: Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

name: Savoury Mini Wraps
description: Soft tortillas rolled with cream cheese, cheddar and a whisper of yeast extract, then sliced into pinwheels. For when sweet food is the last thing you want.
ingredients: 1 tsp yeast extract (optional; it adds salt)
steps: Spread each tortilla thinly with cream cheese, plus a very thin layer of yeast extract if you like it.
Scatter over the cheddar.
Roll each one up tightly, wrap it in foil, and chill for 30 minutes so it firms up and the slices hold together.
Cut each roll into 4 pinwheels.
tip: For the back half of a long day. Cheese keeps for several hours in cool weather; in heat, swap it for salted nut butter.

name: Maple Espresso Gel
description: A homemade caffeinated gel of maple syrup, espresso and salt. About 25 g carbs per serving.
serving_size: 1 gel (about 25 g carbs and 30-40 mg caffeine)
ingredients: 1 shot (30 ml) espresso, or 1/2 tsp instant coffee in 30 ml hot water
steps: Stir the salt into the warm espresso until it dissolves.
Mix it with the maple syrup.
Cool, then pour it into a small reusable soft flask or gel pouch. A 50 ml flask holds both servings.
Shake before sipping.
tip: Save caffeine for the second half of a long race. Around 3 mg per kg of body weight is the upper useful dose for most people; rehearse it in training, never for the first time on race day.

name: Maple Oat Flapjacks
description: Classic chewy flapjacks of oats, butter, brown sugar and maple, cut into bars that travel without crumbling.
steps: Heat the oven to 160°C fan (180°C / 350°F) and line a 20 cm square tin.
Gently melt the butter, sugar, maple syrup and salt together until the sugar dissolves.
Stir in the oats until they're evenly coated.
Press the mixture firmly into the tin and bake for 22-25 minutes, until golden at the edges but still slightly soft in the centre. It firms as it cools, and overbaking makes it rock hard.
Score into 12 while warm and cool completely in the tin before cutting.
tip: Dense, chewy carbs for long, steady efforts. Half a flapjack every 30 minutes is a good starting point.
storage: Keeps for 1 week in an airtight tin.

name: Sweet Potato Mash Pouch
description: Silky sweet potato blended with maple, cinnamon and salt, then squeezed into reusable pouches. Real-food carbs with no chewing.
ingredients: 400 g sweet potato, peeled and cubed
steps: Steam the sweet potato, or microwave it covered with a splash of water, for 8-10 minutes until very soft.
Blend it with the maple syrup, salt, cinnamon and orange juice until completely smooth. Push it through a sieve if needed; fibrous bits block pouch spouts.
Cool it, then fill the pouches.
tip: For when the effort is high and chewing is hard, such as long climbs or the last hour.
storage: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge.

name: Pretzel Nut Butter Bites
description: Mini pretzels sandwiched with salted peanut butter and frozen until firm. Crunchy, salty carbs that cut through sweetness fatigue.
steps: Pair up the pretzels by size.
Spoon or pipe about 1/2 tsp of peanut butter onto one of each pair and sandwich it with the other.
Freeze them on a tray for 20 minutes until firm.
Pack them in a hard box so they don't get crushed.
tip: Salty and crunchy, which is exactly what your mouth wants after hours of sweet food.
storage: Keeps for 2 weeks in the freezer. Eat them straight from frozen or within a few hours.

name: Fig and Sea Salt Rolls
description: Blended dried figs and oats rolled in sesame and flaky salt, then sliced into rounds. Naturally sweet and chewy.
steps: If the figs are very dry, soak them in hot water for 10 minutes, then drain and dry them.
Process the figs, oats, orange zest and salt to a thick, sticky paste.
Roll it into a log 3 cm thick, then roll the log in the sesame seeds and press on some flaky salt.
Chill for 30 minutes and slice into 10 rounds.
tip: Figs are fairly high in fibre, so save these for easy long runs or early in a race rather than the final push.
storage: Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

name: Miso Noodle Broth for Crew Stops
description: A hot, salty flask of miso broth with soft rice vermicelli. For crew stops, night sections and cold backyard-ultra corrals.
steps: Soak the vermicelli in just-boiled water for 3-4 minutes, drain, and snip it into short lengths with scissors so it's easier to drink.
Whisk the miso with a little hot (not boiling) water into a paste; boiling water dulls its flavour.
Top it up with the rest of the hot water and add the soy sauce and sesame oil.
Add the noodles and spring onion and pour everything into an insulated flask. Ask your crew to shake it before pouring.
tip: Hot, salty broth replaces sodium (about 1,000 mg here) and is often the one thing a turned stomach will accept.
